summary: Iter51 backend-only validation of the DEFINITIVE mobile session-expired fix. 16/16 pytest cases PASS in 6.51s against the live preview URL. Validated EVERY claim in the review request: (1) Two-device approval — Device A logs in with key_A → 200 + token; Device B logs in with key_B + same email → 202 with request_id and detail.code='session_pending_approval'. (2) Device A's GET /auth/session-pending lists the new request_id with status='pending' and requesting_key_id=key_B. (3) Device A's POST /auth/session-decide decision=approve → 200 {status:'approved'}. (4) IDEMPOTENCY (5 sequential polls): every POST /auth/session-request-status after approval returns the EXACT SAME session_token, status='approved', email — tokens collected into a set yielded exactly 1 distinct value. (5) WRITE-AFTER-WRITE: immediately after first approval poll returned the token, GET /auth/me with that token as Bearer succeeded on the FIRST try (no retry needed) — confirming the post-insert read-after-write loop (3×50ms) is doing its job. (6) PARALLEL HAMMERING: 10 concurrent ThreadPoolExecutor POSTs to /auth/session-request-status all returned 200, all returned status='approved', all returned the IDENTICAL session_token (set size == 1), no 404/500/duplicate-key errors. (7) After consumption, /auth/session-pending no longer includes the request_id (status flipped from 'pending' → 'approved'). (8) Edge — totally-unknown request_id returns {status:'expired'} with HTTP 200 (NOT 404). (9) Edge — denied request: Device A denies → 200; subsequent polls return {status:'denied'} with NO session_token leaked; 3 repeat polls all return 'denied' (deny idempotent too). (10) DB-level: session_requests doc carries issued_session_token == client-returned token, status='approved', consumed_at populated; user_sessions row exists with correct user_id+device_key_id. (11) Device A's session is NOT disconnected by Device B's approval (/auth/me on A still 200) — matches the bug-report fix claim. (12) Device B's session works (/auth/me on B → 200).

minor.issue: The docstring claims '15 min expiry' but the request itself is INSERTED with a 10-min expires_at (server.py L1058) at /auth/login, and on approval it's RESET to 15 min (server.py L4695). Pre-approval expiry is 10 min, post-approval is 15 min. Probably intentional (give the requesting device extra grace after approval to poll), but the docstring's '15 min' is misleading for the pre-approval window.

Unknown request_id returns {status:'expired'} (HTTP 200). Functionally correct + matches the fix spec, but conflates two distinct states (never-existed vs really-expired). Consider an explicit {status:'unknown'} or {status:'not_found'} for observability — current behaviour leaks zero info to an attacker, which is the security trade-off.

Read-after-write check (L4684-4688) does max 3 × 50ms (150ms total). For a local-write/local-read on a single MongoDB this is overkill (writes are immediately readable), but the guard is harmless. On a replica set with read-preference != primary it would absorb up to 150ms of replication lag. If the hosted Mongo ever switches to secondary preference and lags > 150ms, /auth/me from the client would still fail. Consider documenting the assumption or making the loop count configurable (env var).

If two concurrent polls both see no `issued_session_token` field and both race past the `if not session_token:` branch, both will generate a different secrets.token_urlsafe(32), both will insert a user_sessions row, and both will overwrite issued_session_token on the request — second writer wins, first user_sessions row is orphaned. In practice this is hard to trigger (the 10-parallel hammer test was AFTER the first poll had already populated issued_session_token), so the test didn't expose it. CONSIDER: switch to an atomic find_one_and_update with $setOnInsert semantics, or a unique index on (request_id, issued_session_token) so the second concurrent insert fails fast. Currently the inFlight guard on the frontend prevents this client-side, but the backend invariant should be enforceable on its own.
No rate-limit. A compromised Device A could mass-approve/deny via brute-forced request_ids — though request_ids are 128-bit url-safe tokens so guessing is infeasible. Cosmetic concern only.
Carry-over: server.py is 6436 lines — the session/login flow (lines 920-1100 + 4625-4750) is a strong candidate for extraction into auth_routes.py.

action_items: (Optional) Harden the issued_session_token generation against the rare backend-only race by using find_one_and_update with $setOnInsert (or unique index on issued_session_token).
(Optional) Distinguish 'unknown request_id' from 'really-expired' in the response for observability (currently both return {status:'expired'}). Security-wise OK as-is.
(Optional) Docstring fix on /auth/session-request-status: pre-approval expiry is 10 min (set at /auth/login), reset to 15 min after approval.
(Optional) Make the read-after-write retry count/interval configurable via env vars for future hosted-Mongo replica setups.
critical_code_review_comments: /auth/session-request-status (server.py L4634-4705) — idempotency is implemented by checking `req.get('issued_session_token')` first and only generating + inserting + persisting if absent. On the happy path, the FIRST poll after approval does the insert and DB persistence; all subsequent polls (sequential or parallel) hit the early return and reuse the stored token. The 10-parallel hammer test confirmed this works because the test runs sequentially through test_06 before test_08, so by the time the hammer starts, issued_session_token is already on the request doc. CAVEAT: if two polls arrive simultaneously as the VERY FIRST polls after approval (race window between the approve-write and the first status read), both might miss the token and both might create user_sessions rows — see minor issues. The frontend inFlight guard mitigates this client-side; backend should still be hardened for defense-in-depth.

Write-after-write check (L4684-4688) — 3 retries × 50ms after user_sessions.insert_one. With Mongo on the same supervisor host writing to its primary, this is essentially a no-op (the first read always succeeds). The check is appropriate insurance for replica setups. Cost: max 150ms extra latency on the very first poll after approval. The test_07_auth_me_works_first_try_after_approval verified this works — /auth/me on the issued token succeeded on the first call (no client retry).

/auth/session-pending (L4708-4718) — correctly filters by status='pending' AND expires_at>now_iso AND user_id. After approval/denial, status flips so the row stops appearing. Sort by created_at desc, limit 50 — sensible bounds.

/auth/session-decide (L4726-4746) — atomic update with idempotency-by-status: only updates rows currently in 'pending' state (find filter includes status='pending'); calling decide on an already-approved or already-denied request returns 404 'Demande introuvable ou déjà traitée.' Good. Decision is validated against {'approve','deny'}, anything else → 400. Decided_at is timestamped. Note: there's no audit of WHICH device A's session signed off — only the user_id is checked via get_current_user. Acceptable since 'all of user_id's active devices are equivalent' is the security model.

/auth/login pending-queue branch (L1014-1071) — gates on `requesting_key_id` truthiness; if the requesting device omits device_key_id, the login proceeds normally (no queuing). This is a deliberate fallback for old clients but means a malicious client could simply omit device_key_id to bypass approval. CONSIDER: enforce device_key_id presence for /auth/login post-iter51, or at minimum log a warning when it's absent.

rca of the issue: Original bug: parallel 2.5s-spaced polls + Mongo write-propagation race caused (a) two polls of the same approved request to issue DIFFERENT session_tokens and insert TWO user_sessions rows (frontend would receive token A from poll-1 but use token B from poll-2 → /auth/me with token A fails → mobile shows 'session expired'); (b) the very first /auth/me right after the approval poll could outrun the user_sessions insert visibility → 401 → same symptom. FIX VALIDATION: (1) Idempotency — the request doc now stores issued_session_token on first approval read; every subsequent poll reads it back and reuses it. Verified via 5 sequential + 10 parallel polls → all returned IDENTICAL token (set size 1). (2) Write-after-write — after user_sessions.insert_one, the backend does up to 3 × 50ms find_one(session_token=...) to confirm visibility before returning. Verified: /auth/me with the issued token returned 200 on the FIRST request, no retry, no 401. (3) Edge cases — unknown request_id returns {status:'expired'} (200), denied returns {status:'denied'} (no token leaked), denied is idempotent across repeat polls. (4) No collateral damage — Device A's session remains active after Device B's approval. All 16 tests pass in 6.51s. THE FIX IS CORRECT AND HOLDS UNDER THE TESTED LOAD. Caveat: a hypothetical race exists at the backend level if TWO clients poll for the FIRST time simultaneously before issued_session_token is set — the frontend inFlight guard prevents this in practice but a defense-in-depth find_one_and_update is recommended (see action_items).
